changes: Add a card line stating that three equal angles (AAA) do not prove triangles congruent, because the triangles can differ in size.
Add a card line stating that two equal sides with an angle that is not between them (SSA) do not prove triangles congruent, and include a question on this case.
match.reason: The bank card covers the same four congruence tests at a suitable depth, but it does not teach the two invalid cases (AAA and SSA) that the new point requires, so it needs those additions.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point, mat-tests-congruent-triangles, teaches the SSS, SAS, AAS and RHS tests, but it never explains why AAA and two sides with a non-included angle do not prove congruence, and the brief asks for that. Adding it would mean a new step on the card rather than a small change, so this needs a new point.

draft.title: Congruent triangles
card: Congruent figures are exactly the same shape and size. One can be moved onto the other by sliding, turning or flipping it, so matching sides and angles are equal.
SSS and SAS
SSS: all three sides are equal. SAS: two sides and the angle between them are equal.
AAS and RHS
AAS: two angles and a side are equal, with the side in the same place in both triangles. RHS: both have a right angle, and the hypotenuse and one other side are equal.
Not enough
AAA is not a test: triangles with equal angles can be different sizes. Two sides and an angle that is not between them is not a test either.
draft.remember: Congruent triangles match in shape and size. Check them with SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS.

a.q: Triangle ABC has \(AB = 5\) cm, \(BC = 7\) cm and \(\angle B = 40^{\circ}\). Triangle PQR has \(PQ = 5\) cm, \(QR = 7\) cm and \(\angle Q = 40^{\circ}\). Which test shows they are congruent?
a.why: The equal angle is between the two equal sides in each triangle, so the test is SAS. SSS is tempting, but the third side of each triangle is not given.
a.clue: Where does the angle sit compared with the two sides?

b.q: Triangle DEF has \(DE = 6\) cm, \(EF = 9\) cm and \(\angle D = 30^{\circ}\). Triangle XYZ has \(XY = 6\) cm, \(YZ = 9\) cm and \(\angle X = 30^{\circ}\). Are they shown to be congruent?
opts: No, the angle is not between the two equal sides
No, because only one angle is equal
b.why: In each triangle the 30° angle is at the end of the 6 cm side, but it is not between the 6 cm and 9 cm sides. Two sides and an angle that is not between them is not a congruence test. SAS looks tempting, but it needs the angle between the sides.
b.clue: Find the side that lies opposite the given angle.

b.best: No, the angle is not between the two equal sides

problems.detail: The example is the non-ambiguous case. The side opposite the 30° angle (EF = 9 cm) is longer than the adjacent side (DE = 6 cm), so only one triangle fits these measurements and DEF and XYZ really are congruent, just not by a listed test. A careful student could be misled that such triangles might differ. Use an ambiguous case instead, such as EF = YZ = 4 cm, where 6 sin 30° = 3 < 4 < 6 gives two possible triangles.

The clue 'Find the side that lies opposite the given angle' points students at the wrong feature. The key idea is that the angle is not between the two given sides. In this data, the side opposite the angle being the longer one is exactly what makes the triangle unique.

check.summary: Question b uses a two-sides-and-a-non-included-angle case where the side opposite the angle is the longer one, so the triangles are actually congruent, even though no listed test proves it. Change the numbers to an ambiguous case (for example EF = YZ = 4 cm) and fix the clue. Question a is fine.
